messages.subject: Re: Proportional Bar Charts
messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

The reason is simple, but fairly subtle - it's because of the default
grouping behaviour.  By default ggplot splits up the data according to
the combination of levels of all the categorical variables on the plot
- so in your case you get a dataset for each bar, and so the density
is just n / n = 1.  The way to get around this is to override the
default grouping so that there is a single group for the whole
dataset:

qplot(cut, data = diamonds, geom = "bar")
qplot(cut, ..density.., data = diamonds, geom = "bar")
qplot(cut, ..density.., data = diamonds, geom = "bar", group = 1)

I realise this isn't very obvious, but I don't think I can change the
default behaviour with out breaking things in other places.

Regards,

Hadley

Vitalie.

messages.subject_clean: how to use facet to "zoom" part of a time series?
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to tackle the following: consider weekly measurements
between 1990 and 2005. Annual statistics shall be visualised with a
sequence of boxplots. The years 1998-2000 stand out by their generally
high values.

Facetting by year allows me to single out the period 1998-2000 so that
its high values won't flatten down all the remaining boxplots. There
will thus be three facet for the periods 1990-97, 98-00, and 2001 and
later

While facet_wrap offers to separate the y-axes (and have them adjusted
to the different y-ranges), it will allot equal horizontal space to
each of the periods: 1990-97 will show narrow boxes (all have to fit
into the facet), 1998-00 wide  boxes (only three years to occupy the
panel width) and so on.

Facet_grid, in turn, allows to define "space=free" and have the facet
width automatically adjust to the number of categories contained.
However, in facet_grid, all facets of a row have to share one y-axis.
Which was to be avoided in the first place.

Any suggestions greatly appreciated. I'm not too familiar with the
ggplot2 grammar yet, so I guess I'm just missing some straightforward
solution. After all, the package seems to be the coolest plotting tool
around!

best regards
Ivo

messages.subject: New version of ggplot2, 0.8.1
messages.body_plain:
ggplot2 ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot2 is a plotting system for R, based on the grammar of graphics,
which tries to take the good parts of base and lattice graphics and
avoid bad parts. It takes care of many of the fiddly details
that make plotting a hassle (like drawing legends) as well as
providing a powerful model of graphics that makes it easy to produce
complex multi-layered graphics.

Find out more at http://had.co.nz/ggplot2, and check out the nearly 500
examples of ggplot in use.  If you're interested, you can also sign up to
the ggplot2 mailing list at http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2, or track
development at  http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2

ggplot2 0.8.1  (2008-12-12)
----------------------------------------

New features

* new labs, xlab & ylab functions for easily modifying axis labels and
legend titles
* qplot now guesses what geom you want based on the position
aesthetics that you provide:
  * both x & y: scatterplot
  * only x: histogram
  * only y: scatterplot of seq_along(y) vs y
* scale_datetime: a first attempt at a scale for date time objects of
class POSIXt

Aesthetic improvements

* legends should now work in cases where you have multiple layers the
use the same geom and have different aesthetic mappings
* theme: new theme setting legend.key.size determines size of keys in legend
* theme: new theme setting plot.margins to control the plot margins
* tweaks to plot and legend layout

Other minor improvements

* geom_point warns if missing values present in data and not displayed on plot
* geom_smooth gives a more accurate warning when you have incorrectly
specified the grouping
* geom_smooth will switch to an alternative smoothing method
(mgcv::gam(y ~ s(x, bs = "cr"))), when there are more than 1000
observations
* layers gain a legend argument, which allow you to force the layer
either into (TRUE) or out of (FALSE) the legend

Bug fixes

* coord_equal now calculates scales correctly again
* coord_flip: flips axes labels again too
* coord_trans fix bug where transformation incorrect
* facet_grid: fix bug where tick labels where being produced outside
the range of the axes
* facet_wrap: fixed bug with ncol = 1 or nrow = 1
* facet_wrap: labels correctly clipped to axis ranges
* facet_wrap: labels will match panels even when factor levels are not
in alphabetical order
* facet_wrap: now works when a layer doesn't contain every level of
the faceting variables
* geom_abline should now work in a wider variety of situations
* geom_smooth now gives correct asymmetric standard errors with
generalised linear models (thanks to Thierry Onkelinx)
* geom_vline and geom_hline now correctly transform their intercepts
if the scale is transformed
* geom_vline and geom_hline: now use xintercept and yintercept instead
of intercept
* legend.position and legend.justification work again
* position_dodge now works for any number of elements with smaller
widths, not just 2!
* scale_discrete_position: does a better job of calculating axis
limits when plotting a mixture of continuous and discrete values (e.g.
with geom_jitter)
* summary: tweaks to improve output

--

>  geom_ribbon(x=x,ymin=low,ymax=high,fill="red",colour="maroon")

This is a probably bug in qplot - but the bug is that it doesn't
complain that you're trying to mix data defined in d with data defined
in the global environment.  I'd suggest you do something like this:

rib <- within(subset(d, ind == "y1"), {
  low <- y1 - 1
  high <- y1 + 1
})

qplot(x, values, data = d, colour = ind, geom = "line") +
 geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), data = rib, fill="black",
colour="pink")

Generally with ggplot, it's best to work with data in data frames -
then it's easy to be absolutely explicit about where everything is
coming from.

Hadley

L2eV <- # converts wavelength to energy
function (lambda)
{
    cel <- 299792458
    h <- 6.62606896e-34
    ee <- 1.602176487e-19
    eV <- h * cel/ee/lambda
    eV
}

valuesLambda<-c(400,500,600,700,800,1000)*1e-3 # custom values for the
second axis
valuesL2eV<- L2eV(valuesLambda*1e-6)  # corresponding positions in the
plot units

my.data <- data.frame(energy <- seq(1, 3, length=100), y = (energy)^2)

### base graphics ###

with(my.data, {
plot(energy, y, t="l",xlab=expression("resonance energy / eV"),
ylab=expression("resonance width / eV"))
axis(3, at=valuesL2eV ,labels = paste(valuesLambda))
mtext(expression("wavelength / "*mu*m), line=2)
})

### lattice graphics ###
xyplot(y~energy, data=my.data, t="l", scales=list(y=list(tck=c(1, 0)),
x=list(tck=c(1, 0))),
par.settings = list(layout.widths = list(ylab = 1,axis.right= 1.5),
layout.heights = list(xlab = 1,axis.top= 1.5)) ,
xlab=expression("resonance energy / eV"), ylab=expression("resonance
width / eV"),

("wavelength / "*mu*m), pos=3, offset=2)

    })

In a situation where outliers are not wanted to show up in a boxplot,
ylim() is a handy shortcut to set the range of the y-axis. However, it
does not simply clip the figure but instead has the boxplots stats
calculated for the subset of data that fits into the desired range.
While boxplot_stats does display a warning ("Removed ... rows
containing missing values..." this same warning is triggered by true
NAs in the dataset. The messy user = me ;) - might then ignore the
warning with the NAs in mind, being unaware that boxplots are drawn
for a trimmed dataset.

A corresponding extension of the warning message could be helpful.

best regards

Dear all,

Thank you for the suggestions. It seems to me that the easiest
solution
would be to consider the second axis as an external object added for
convenience, much like raw grid commands can be used to fine-tune
lattice

much

scale for "Value of $1 Invested" is preferred (so that the slope
corresponds to the percent return in any period), but the y axis
rarely goes above 10, which makes the 10^n notation awkward.

dts <- seq(as.Date("2008-1-1"), as.Date("2008-12-31"), by="day")

require(reshape)
mda <- melt(da, id.vars = "Date")

ytx <- 2^(0:4)
p <- ggplot(mda, aes(Date, value)) +
     scale_x_date("") +
     scale_y_log10("Value of $1 Investment", breaks = ytx, labels =
ytx)
p + geom_line(aes(colour=factor(variable))) +
    opts(title="An Unreal Performance") +
    scale_colour_manual("Manager", values=c("red","purple")) +
    facet_grid(variable~., scales = "free_y")

-----

plot.
